title: No longer mourn for me: the mortality group
short: The first of a group (71-74) in which the poet contemplates his own death and asks the friend how to remember him.
body: Sonnets 71-74 imagine the poet's death and burial and set his mortal body against his surviving verse. Sonnet 71 is paradoxical: it asks the friend to mourn only briefly, and even to forget, out of love. Critics read the self-effacement differently: as tender selflessness, as a manipulative plea that guarantees remembrance (Vendler), or as anxiety about the friend's social shame. Christina Rossetti's sonnet 'Remember' (written 1849, published 1862) is a later poem on the same theme: it asks to be remembered, then releases the beloved to forget.

title: the surly sullen bell
short: The church bell tolled to announce a death; the friend should mourn no longer than it rings.
body: In Elizabethan parish practice a 'passing bell' was rung when someone was dying, and a knell after death, to call for prayers; the number of strokes could indicate the sex and age of the dead person. The bell 'gives warning' (announces) to the world. 'Surly' and 'sullen' (gloomy, heavy) personify it. Compare 2 Henry IV 1.1: news of death 'Sounds ever after as a sullen bell, / Remember'd tolling a departing friend'. Donne's Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (1624), Meditation 17, is the most famous later meditation on the custom.

title: vile world with vilest worms to dwell
short: The poet flees a vile world to live with even viler worms in the grave; the Quarto spells 'vildest'.
body: The repetition 'vile ... vilest' (Quarto 'vilde ... vildest', a common Elizabethan form of the word) makes the grave a comic-grim downgrade from a world already despised. Worms feeding on the buried body are a biblical and medieval commonplace ('though after my skin worms destroy this body', Job 19:26). The word 'fled' suggests a flight from bad company, an escape that turns out to be no better.

title: if you read this line, remember not
short: The poem imagines its reader after the poet's death and asks him to forget the hand that wrote the very line he reads.
body: The paradox is that the request for forgetting is made in writing that will survive, and by being read it cannot help prompting memory. 'The hand that writ it' presents the manuscript as a physical relic of the dead writer. Many critics see the sonnet's self-erasure as rhetorically double: the more the poet asks to be forgotten, the more he is remembered. The reference to the reader is common in the mortality sonnets (compare 74, 'When thou reviewest this').

title: make you woe
short: 'Woe' is used as an adjective: woeful, sorrowful.
body: Shakespeare and his contemporaries could use 'woe' predicatively, as in 'make you woe' (make you sad), a use the OED records. The rhyme 'so / woe' closes the second quatrain with a plain, almost conversational phrase that contrasts with the formality of the opening. Readers should not take it as the noun: the sense is simply 'that you should be sad'. The same adjectival use appears elsewhere in Shakespeare, for example in The Tempest ('I am woe for't', 5.1), and it gives the end of the octave an informal, spoken quality.

title: compounded am with clay
short: Mixed or mingled with the earth of the grave: the biblical return of the body to dust.
body: 'Compounded' means mixed into one substance. The image draws on Genesis 3:19, 'for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return', and on the Burial Service in the Book of Common Prayer ('earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust'). 'Perhaps' (l. 10) is quietly significant: the poet does not know when he will die, and the friend's reading may come soon or late.

title: rehearse
short: To repeat or recite aloud; the friend should not even speak the poet's name.
body: 'Rehearse' in Shakespeare usually means to repeat, recount or say over (from Old French rehercier, to harrow again). To 'rehearse' a name might also suggest naming in prayers for the dead or in an epitaph. The poet calls his name 'poor', in keeping with the self-depreciation of the Rival Poet sonnets that follow (78-86). The request not to name the poet is the more striking because the sonnet itself is the place where his memory would survive; Sonnet 72 develops it into the wish that his name be buried with his body.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'rehearse'

title: let your love even with my life decay
short: Let your love die exactly when my life does: an apparently selfless request that is also a test of love.
body: 'Even with' means at the same moment as, or equally with. The line reverses the sequence's usual hope that love outlasts life (compare Sonnet 116). Booth and Vendler note the emotional pressure of such a request, since the friend who loves cannot obey it, so the line both releases and binds him. The phrasing turns the language of mortality ('decay') onto love itself, so that the friend's affection is to be buried with the poet.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets, Edited with Analytic Commentary (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1977), commentary on Sonnet 71, l. 12
Helen Vendler, The Art of Shakespeare's Sonnets (Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press, 1997), essay on Sonnet 71

title: the wise world ... mock you
short: The real reason for forgetting appears: the cynical 'wise' world would mock the friend for grieving over so poor a man.
body: 'Wise' is ironic: worldly, knowing, cynical. 'Look into your moan' means pry into, examine the cause of, your lament. The couplet suggests a social gap between the poet and the noble friend, so that grief for the poet would expose the friend to ridicule. Critics divide on whether the tone is bitter (the world's scorn) or loving (protection of the friend); Sonnet 72 continues the thought ('My name be buried where my body is').
